meta.title: Liber AL vel Legis — Research Status

summary: Ongoing investigative research into the historical, textual, cryptographic, and esoteric dimensions of Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law), received by Aleister Crowley in Cairo, April 1904.

areas.title: Historical Context & Cairo Working
findings: Rose Crowley's role as unwitting channel: she identified the intelligence as 'Aiwass, the minister of Hoor-paar-kraat' after passing tests about Horus drawn from the Budge Egyptian dictionary
The Cairo Working took place April 7–9, 1904 — exactly one hour per day at noon — in the Bolak district apartment
The Stele of Revealing (Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu) was exhibit 666 in the Boulaq Museum — Crowley claimed this was beyond coincidence
Rose had no known background in Egyptian religion prior to the working
gaps: Verify exact Boulaq Museum exhibit numbering records — is '666' independently documented?
Primary sources on Rose Crowley's psychological state during this period
Cross-reference with Crowley's diaries vs. later autobiographical accounts for discrepancies

areas.title: Manuscript & Textual Analysis
findings: The original handwritten manuscript is held at the Warburg Institute, London — 65 pages in Crowley's hand
Chapter III line 47 famously contains the instruction 'the comment' which has been interpreted as forbidding commentary
Multiple published editions contain variant readings — the 1909 'Equinox' publication vs. later OTO editions differ in punctuation and capitalization
The manuscript contains marginal annotations added by Crowley at later dates, creating layered textual strata
gaps: Full collation of all published editions against the Warburg manuscript — not yet complete
Dating of the marginal annotations — which are contemporaneous (1904) vs. retrospective?
Analysis of the grid/cipher in Chapter III (v. 47) — does it correspond to any known cipher system?

areas.title: Egyptian Religious Sources
findings: Nuit (Ch. I), Hadit (Ch. II), and Ra-Hoor-Khuit (Ch. III) correspond to Nut, Behedti/Hadit, and Ra-Horakhty in Egyptian religion
The Stele dates to the 26th Dynasty (c. 680 BCE) and depicts Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu before Ra-Hoor-Khuit
The 'Adoration of the Stele' (Chapter I, verses 24–30) closely parallels the funerary text on the actual stele
Hadit as a form of Horus-Behedti (the winged disk) appears in Edfu temple texts — connection to the 'point within the circle' symbolism
gaps: Comparative analysis with the Pyramid Texts and Coffin Texts for Nuit / Nut theology
Is the 'Khabs am Pekht' (Ch. III) traceable to a specific Egyptian source or is it Crowley's invention?
Academic Egyptological assessment of Crowley's Egyptian attributions

areas.title: Cryptographic & Cipher Elements
findings: Chapter III v. 47 contains a 7×7 grid with the instruction 'fill the grid' — the intended method remains disputed
gaps: Survey all published attempts to solve the cipher (Gunther, Duquette, etc.)
Apply modern cryptanalytic methods to the grid
Investigate whether the grid relates to Enochian or Cabalistic systems

areas.title: Commentary Tradition
findings: Crowley produced at least three major commentaries: the 1909 notes, the 'Old Comment', and the 'New Comment' (1920s)
The 'New Comment' was suppressed by Crowley himself for years, calling it potentially dangerous
Frieda Harris (artist of the Thoth Tarot) corresponded with Crowley extensively about Ch. I geometry
Kenneth Grant's commentary tradition (Typhonian OTO) significantly diverges from Thelemic orthodoxy
gaps: Locate and review the 'AB' (Aleister Blackwood?) commentary fragments at the Yorke Collection
Assess Jane Wolfe's diary notes on the Book from Cefalu
Map the full lineage of unauthorized/marginal commentaries

areas.title: Prophetic & Aeonics Claims
findings: Crowley interpreted the Book as heralding the Aeon of Horus, replacing the Aeon of Osiris (Christianity)
The 'word of the law is Thelema' (Greek: θέλημα = will) — Rabelais' Thélème was a known source
The Book's declaration 'Every man and every woman is a star' has been read as proto-individualist philosophy
Crowley's identification with the Beast 666 and Babalon developed substantially AFTER the Cairo Working — were these retroactive?
gaps: Timeline of Crowley's development of the Aeonics doctrine — how much changed between 1904 and 1913?
Comparison with other 'received texts' of the era (Oahspe, Urantia Book, Vatinian Oracle) for structural parallels
Critical assessment of fulfilled vs. unfulfilled prophecies

areas.title: Reception & Cultural Impact
gaps: Trace the Book's influence on 20th-century counterculture (Jack Parsons, L. Ron Hubbard, Kenneth Anger, Jimmy Page)
Academic reception — when did scholars begin treating Liber AL as a serious object of study?
Legal history — OTO intellectual property disputes over the text

areas.title: Philosophical & Ethical Analysis
findings: 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law' — the 'True Will' doctrine distinguishes this from libertinism
The Book explicitly endorses a warrior ethic and rejects pity/compassion in ways that are ethically problematic
Chapter II's nihilistic passages ('There is no bond that can unite the divided but love') sit in tension with Chapter III's militarism
gaps: Systematic comparison with Nietzsche (whom Crowley read) — similarities and divergences in Will doctrine
How do contemporary Thelemites reconcile Ch. III's violence with modern ethics?
Is there a coherent ontology in the three chapters or are they intentionally contradictory?

keyQuestions: Did the Cairo Working represent a genuine anomalous experience, psychological event, literary fabrication, or some combination?
What is the relationship between the Book's theology and Crowley's prior study of Kabbalah, Freemasonry, and Golden Dawn material?
Can the cipher in Chapter III be definitively solved, and what does this reveal about the text's authorship?
How should the Book be read: as prophecy, as poetry, as magical instruction, or as a philosophical treatise?
What is the status of the Warburg manuscript and can a definitive critical edition be produced?
